CASE-001Professional Project

SSO Discovery & Integrations Hub

Internship ProjectCloudflare

A cloud-native way to check how ready a vendor's application is for single sign-on, and to keep that picture in one place.

SSOSAMLOIDCCloud-NativeAutomation
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Working out whether a vendor supports SAML or OIDC means reading its public documentation, one vendor at a time, and the answers end up scattered.

The Solution

Automated discovery that analyzes public vendor documentation for SAML and OIDC support and produces a structured readiness report, giving centralized visibility into integrations.

My Contribution

I designed the system, defined the requirements and workflows, directed AI coding agents on the implementation, and handled integration and testing.

Technical Concepts

  • Vendor Authentication Readiness
  • SAML / OIDC Discovery
  • Documentation Analysis
  • Centralized Visibility
  • Cloud-Native Automation
CASE-002Professional Project

AI Access Troubleshooter

PrototypeCloudflare

A read-only AI assistant that turns an access request into a structured diagnosis: the likely missing piece, a root cause with a confidence level, next steps for the admin, and a draft reply to the requester. It is a prototype, and its diagnoses have not yet been checked against live tickets.

IAMAI AgentsInput ValidationGuardrails
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Access requests are often vague, and a confident-sounding guess can send someone the wrong fix.

The Solution

A structured intake, a set of known failure patterns to check against, and guardrails. It never grants or changes access, and it says when it couldn't verify a fact.

My Contribution

I defined the requirements and safeguards, directed AI coding agents on the implementation, and tested it on synthetic tickets, including attempts to get it to skip checks.

Technical Concepts

  • Structured Intake
  • Failure-Pattern Matching
  • Confidence Levels
  • Read-Only Guardrails
  • Hallucination Mitigation
CASE-003Personal Project

EML Phishing Triage Analyzer

Implemented

A small, explainable command-line tool that reads a .eml file and reports why an email looks suspicious, with a low, medium, or high verdict.

PythonEmail SecurityCLIpytest
View On GitHub
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Triage of a suspicious email is repetitive: the same headers, links, and attachments get checked by hand every time.

The Solution

The tool checks the email against a set of weighted rules and adds them into a score. Every point in the score comes with a reason, so you can see why an email was flagged.

My Contribution

A personal project, published on my GitHub with synthetic sample emails and a test suite.

Technical Concepts

  • SPF / DKIM / DMARC Results
  • Reply-To & Return-Path Mismatch
  • Lookalike Domains
  • Link Analysis
  • Risky Attachments
  • Explainable Scoring

What It Checks

  • Whether SPF, DKIM, or DMARC checks failed.
  • Sender, Reply-To, and Return-Path mismatches.
  • Lookalike or brand-impersonating sender domains.
  • Link tricks: display text versus real destination, raw IP links, punycode, URL shorteners.
  • Risky attachment types: executables, scripts, macro-enabled Office files.
  • Urgency or account-threat wording.

Safety & Limitations

  • Read-only: it never opens attachments, follows links, or makes network requests.
  • Heuristics, not a verdict oracle: false positives and false negatives are expected.
  • No sandboxing or live URL reputation lookups.
CASE-004Personal Project

Detection Engineering Lab

Implemented

Experimental detection rules applied to sign-in and account events, using fictional events only.

Detection RulesAlert TriageSynthetic Data
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Detection logic is easier to understand when you can watch a rule fire, and see when it correctly stays quiet.

The Solution

A set of fictional event timelines is run through predefined rules in the browser. Each alert shows its severity, why it triggered, and the investigation steps that would follow.

My Contribution

Technical Concepts

  • Unusual Location

  • Activity Volume
  • Severity
CASE-005Personal Project

Secure Password Generator

Implemented

A browser password generator with configurable length and character sets, cryptographic randomness, and an entropy estimate.

Web CryptoEntropyBrowser
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Many simple generators use predictable randomness, or pick characters in a slightly biased way.

The Solution

Characters are chosen with the browser's cryptographic random source using unbiased selection, every selected character type is guaranteed to appear, and the estimated entropy is shown.

My Contribution

Built for this portfolio with AI-assisted development, from requirements I defined. Passwords are never logged, sent, or stored.

Technical Concepts

  • Cryptographic Randomness
  • Rejection Sampling
  • Entropy
  • Character Sets
CASE-006Professional Project

PhishER Ticket Analysis

Completed · July 2026Austin Industries

A review of 596 user-reported emails to separate confirmed phishing from everything else and find the patterns attackers kept reusing.

KnowBe4 PhishERExcel
≈75%Of Reported Emails Were Confirmed Phishing
448 Confirmed Phishing148 Other Reports
Read The Case StudyHide The Case Study

The Problem

Turn a queue of user-reported emails into answers: how many were real threats, and what did the real ones have in common?

The Solution

A structured review of every ticket, then trend analysis of the confirmed threats in Excel.

My Contribution

I reviewed the tickets, separated confirmed phishing from the rest, and analyzed the confirmed threats for patterns.

Technical Concepts

  • Phishing Trends
  • Malicious Sender Behavior
  • Abuse Of Trusted Services

How I Approached It

  1. Reviewed 596 user-reported email security tickets in KnowBe4 PhishER.
  2. Separated the confirmed phishing threats from the rest of the reports.
  3. Used Excel to evaluate the confirmed threats for phishing trends, malicious sender behavior, and abuse of trusted services.

What I Found

  • 448 of the 596 reports (about 75%) were confirmed phishing threats.
  • The confirmed threats shared recurring attack patterns, including abuse of trusted services.

How It Was Used

The findings supported threat detection, security awareness initiatives, and email security recommendations.
